courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Projecting Gaussians to splats and sorting them by tile
md: The sort is per tile, by each Gaussian's center depth, not per pixel. Where two large splats interpenetrate, the true order can differ from pixel to pixel, so blending is approximate. The paper notes this error becomes negligible as splats shrink toward pixel size, and lists sudden order switches (popping) as a limitation.

courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: Hazard pointers and epochs: stop reuse while anyone looks
md: "Garbage collection solves ABA" is a common misconception that Michael calls out. GC prevents ABA caused by *reuse*, but if a program moves the same nodes back and forth between two lock-free stacks, a node can leave and return to the same position with perfect GC. Ask whether the algorithm is ABA-safe under GC first; only then do hazard pointers or epochs make it ABA-safe without GC.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Reporting an ablation people can trust
md: Report per-stage deltas with intervals, the paired test and effect size, win/loss counts, interaction cells for stages that depend on each other, and cost, all on one stated harness. A bare column of mean scores invites the wrong conclusion.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Mass assignment and property-level authorization
md: Allowlists rot in one direction: new fields. A blocklist that forbids `isAdmin` today silently allows `isOwner` added next quarter. An allowlist forgets a new field by leaving it read-only, which fails safe.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: NTLM: challenge and response, and why the hash is enough
md: NTLM never sends the password, but its proof is computed only from the unsalted NT hash plus a server challenge. So the hash is the password. Move to NTLMv2 only, then to Kerberos, and watch 4776 and the 4624 package name.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: DCSync: asking a domain controller for every password
md: 4662 is only written if Directory Service Access auditing is on **and** the domain object's SACL asks for it. Many domains have neither, and then DCSync leaves no Security log trace at all. Check before you need it.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: The exploit lifecycle: bug, primitive, leak, control, payload
md: Exploitation is a ladder of capabilities: bug, primitive, leak, control, payload. Every mitigation removes or weakens one rung, and the earlier the rung, the more bug-specific and costly the attacker's workaround.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: An agent benchmark is a task, an environment and a grader
md: An agent benchmark score is a property of **model + harness + environment + grader + metric**. Change any one and the number moves. Most of this course is about how each part shapes the score.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: A minimal harness: stop conditions, errors and budgets
md: Do not retry a tool blindly. Re-running a failed `git push` or a payment call can duplicate a side effect. Retry the model API transport freely, but report tool failures back to the model and let it decide, or make the tool itself idempotent, meaning running it twice has the same effect as running it once (for example, a payment call that carries a unique request key the server uses to ignore duplicates).

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Consolidation and forgetting: reflection, decay and deletion
md: Deletion must follow lineage. Keep source pointers on every derived memory (Generative Agents already stores the cited records for each reflection) so that deleting a source can find and rewrite or delete every reflection, summary and merged fact that contains it. Also delete the embeddings and any copies in logs.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Multi-turn rollouts: one sequence, two authors, one loss mask
md: A common bug: tokenizing the final transcript string again for training instead of keeping the exact token ids that were sampled. Re-tokenizing can merge tokens differently at the boundaries between model text and tool text, so the log-probabilities you train on no longer match the ones the policy produced, and the mask can land on the wrong positions.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Getting data out: images, links, tool calls
md: For every LLM feature, list the ways out: rendered images, links, tools that make network requests, and the user. Close the ones you do not need and allowlist the rest. Without a way out, stolen context stays put.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Data and model poisoning: backdoors you cannot see
md: Poisoning is a supply chain attack on data. Verify integrity with hashes, record provenance, and treat a model from an unknown trainer like a binary from an unknown publisher.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: GNoME: active learning with DFT, and what counts as new
md: Active learning turns DFT from a verifier into a teacher: each round's results, including failures, retrain the filter, so the hit rate per DFT call keeps rising.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Attacks, limits, and content credentials for images
md: Watermarks are statistical evidence woven into content; content credentials are signed claims attached to a file. Metadata is easy to strip but cryptographically strong; watermarks survive some edits but can be scrubbed, spoofed or never applied. Real deployments combine them.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Isolation Forest: anomalies split off in fewer random cuts
md: Isolation Forest scores a point by how few random axis-parallel cuts it takes to isolate it, normalized by c(n). It is fast (training is O(t psi log psi) and needs no distances), works on a small subsample, and is strongest for global anomalies far from all the data.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: APIs from zero: REST, GraphQL and what a request carries
md: An API request carries two questions: who is calling (authentication, answered by a credential in the request) and may they do this to this object (authorization, answered by the server on every request).

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Retired grants (implicit and password) and client credentials
md: Modern OAuth in one line: authorization code with PKCE for anything with a user, client credentials for machine to machine, and nothing that puts tokens in URLs or passwords in clients.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Case: Storm-0558 and the forged Microsoft tokens (2023)
md: A valid signature is only as good as the question "is this key one that this issuer uses for this kind of token?" RFC 8725 says it plainly: check that the keys belong to the issuer. And signing keys are crown jewels: rotate them, retire them, alert on their age, and log every use.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Secure code review: what a reviewer looks for
md: Review the flows, not the lines. For every value from outside, follow it to each sink and check the control at each trust boundary. Then ask the questions a tool cannot: should this exist, and who may use it?

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: CVE assignment and CNAs: who names a vulnerability
md: Fewer CVEs is not the same as fewer vulnerabilities. A vendor that fixes bugs silently looks clean while customers' scanners have nothing to match and never flag the old version. Judge vendors by how fast and how well they publish, not by the count.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: LSNs, pageLSN and the two tables recovery rebuilds
md: Do not mix up pageLSN and recLSN. In the example, P1 was first dirtied at LSN 10 and last changed at 60, so its recLSN is 10 while its pageLSN is 60. recLSN says where redo for the page might need to start; pageLSN says which changes the page already contains.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: A toy run: how the input type flips the top result
md: Simplified: real embeddings are not interpretable feature lists, and the size of the effect varies by model and corpus. The toy shows the direction of the failure, not its typical magnitude. Lesson 5 is about measuring the magnitude on your data.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Why waiting on threads is expensive and coroutines are cheap
md: Async does not make one request faster. It makes **waiting cheap**: a waiting connection costs a small saved object instead of a blocked OS thread with its own stack, so a few threads can serve many thousands of mostly idle connections.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Compare-and-swap: write only if nothing changed, else retry
md: CAS compares values, not history. If the value goes from A to B and back to A between your load and your CAS, the CAS succeeds as if nothing happened. For a counter that is harmless. For pointers in lock-free data structures (structures built from atomics instead of locks) it can be a real bug, the **ABA problem**, which has its own course later.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Who are you, prove it, and what may you do?
md: Identification is a claim, authentication is proof of the claim, authorization is permission. MFA means two different *kinds* of factor, not two secrets of the same kind.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: After login: session tokens, fixation, expiry and logout
md: A session token is a password with an expiry date. Make it random (64+ bits), send it only as a Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite cookie, replace it at login, expire it on the server, and destroy it on the server at logout.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Orchestrator, parallel subagents and context isolation
md: More subagents is not automatically better. Anthropic's early agents spawned 50 subagents for simple queries and distracted each other with updates. Their prompts now embed effort rules: simple fact-finding gets 1 agent with 3 to 10 tool calls, direct comparisons get 2 to 4 subagents with 10 to 15 calls each, and complex research uses more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: On-demand capacity: tokens per minute and the max_tokens trap
md: Specific burndown rates, default quotas and tier prices change as models launch. Treat any number you remember as stale and read the current quota page and model card before you size a workload.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Running ternary models fast: I2_S, lookup tables, real numbers
md: Loading the 2B4T checkpoint in Hugging Face `transformers` (the standard Python model library) saves memory but gives no speed or energy gain; the model card says the efficiency needs the dedicated bitnet.cpp kernels.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: B+trees update in place, and random writes pay for it
md: A B+tree's write cost is set by the **page**, not the row: a random small update rewrites a whole page at a random location. Reads are cheap because each key lives in exactly one place.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: The buffer pool: frames, a page table, pins and dirty pages
md: A buffer pool is a write-back page cache owned by the database. On a miss it must evict some *unpinned* page, and write it out first if it is *dirty*. Everything else in this course is about choosing that page well.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Entropy patching: spend compute where the next byte is hard
md: Entropy patching spends a global step where the next byte is hard to predict and lets cheap local layers handle predictable runs. The threshold sets the average patch size, and therefore the compute.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Safe wrappers over unsafe code: split_at_mut and soundness
md: Audit unsafe code at the module boundary. Keep fields that unsafe code trusts private, check every invariant before the unsafe block (as `assert!(mid <= len)` does), and write a SAFETY comment that names the invariant.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Where a line may live: sets, ways and tags
md: Capacity is set by size, conflicts by associativity and address bits. A bigger cache fixes capacity misses; more ways or a less regular stride fixes conflict misses; nothing but prefetching (loading lines before the program asks for them, lesson 4) hides cold misses.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Limitations, and tracing circuits yourself
md: An attribution graph explains one prompt in one replacement model. It is not proof of a general algorithm, it is silent about attention's choices, and any path through error nodes is unexplained. State those limits whenever you report a circuit.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: XSS: when your page runs someone else's code
md: An `HttpOnly` session cookie does not make XSS harmless. It stops script from *reading* the cookie, so the attacker cannot take the session home. But the injected script does not need the cookie value: it sends requests from the victim's own browser, and the browser attaches the cookie for it.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Detecting and responding to client-side attacks
md: Prevention lives in code (encode, sanitise, safe sinks, tokens, allowlists). Detection lives mostly in the browser (CSP and Trusted Types reports) and in monitoring of what your pages load. A team that only watches server logs is blind to DOM XSS and skimmers.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: IAM from zero: users, groups, roles and the JSON policy
md: IAM starts from deny. A request is allowed only if some applicable policy explicitly allows it and no applicable policy explicitly denies it. Write policies as a list of what is needed, never as a list of what to forbid.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Catching misconfigurations early: infrastructure as code and CSPM
md: Scanners produce a lot of findings, and most teams drown in them. Rank by what an attacker could do: public exposure of sensitive data, wildcard IAM on roles reachable from the internet, IMDSv1 on internet-facing instances and disabled logging come before "detailed monitoring is off". A posture tool is only as good as the triage behind it.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Arrow in memory: buffers, validity bitmaps and offsets
md: Arrow is not a file format for long-term storage like Parquet. Arrow data is laid out for fast random access and computation and is normally uncompressed in memory (the IPC format allows only optional LZ4 or ZSTD buffer compression); Parquet is encoded and compressed for small size on disk. A typical pipeline reads Parquet and decodes it into Arrow-style (or engine-specific) column vectors.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Inlining: removing a call unlocks every other optimization
md: Inlining matters less for the call it removes than for what it enables: constant folding, dead code removal and vectorization inside the merged body. It costs code size, and it only works when the callee's body is visible in the same compilation.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: The observe-act loop: screenshots in, mouse and keyboard out
md: Misconception: the model "sees" the screen continuously. It sees only the screenshots you return, at the moments you return them. If a dialog pops up after your capture, the model does not know about it until the next screenshot.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: How loom takes over the scheduler and walks every schedule
md: Every source of non-determinism must come from loom: no real time, randomness or I/O inside `loom::model`. Determinism is what lets loom replay a schedule and flip one choice at a time.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: What a consistency model promises, and why replicas break it
md: Model A is **stronger** than model B when every history A allows is also allowed by B (A is a subset of B). Stronger models rule out more surprising results, and usually cost more coordination, latency or availability.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Hot keys: perfect key balance, unbalanced traffic
md: Consistent hashing balances keys. Hot keys need a different tool: copies (replication, client caches) for read-hot keys, splitting for write-hot keys, and miss coalescing for keys that expire under load.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Backtracking search with forward checking and MRV
md: Choose the **variable** that is most likely to fail, and the **value** that is most likely to succeed. Every variable must be assigned eventually, so failing early on the hardest one costs nothing and prunes the most. But only one solution is needed, so values should keep the most options open.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: What ships in an image: base images, distroless and scanning
md: Misconception: "we scan, so our images are safe". A scanner only knows published vulnerabilities in recognised packages. It does not find your own code's bugs, a backdoored but unlisted dependency, or a secret left in a layer unless a secret scanner runs too.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: RBAC: roles, bindings and the permissions that escalate
md: Misconception: "they can only create pods, not read Secrets". Pod creation lets them mount any Secret in the namespace into a pod they control and read it from inside. Treat create-pods as read-all-secrets for that namespace, unless admission policy restricts what pods may mount.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Secrets: base64 is not encryption
md: Misconception: "our Secrets are encrypted because they look scrambled in kubectl". That is base64. Check whether the API server has --encryption-provider-config at all, and whether identity is first; the docs list both as signs that encryption at rest is not enabled.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: What an image actually is: layers, unions and digests
md: An image is an ordered list of content-addressed changesets plus a config. Everything else follows from that one sentence: identical layers are stored and transferred once, a deletion only adds a marker, and changing any layer invalidates every layer after it. Order your build steps from least to most frequently changing.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Resolving the second one and those against what was shown
md: References point at a response, not at the conversation. Store the ordered ids you displayed, with a version, and resolve ordinals, attributes and *those* against that stored list.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: CoT monitors, and what training against them does
md: Misconception: "the monitor flags less often after training, so the model behaves better." A falling flag rate is what both genuine improvement and obfuscation look like. Without an independent ground-truth check of the behavior, you cannot tell them apart.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Packing the pair: special tokens, segments and the 512-token limit
md: A larger max_length is not free and not always possible. Position embeddings fix the hard limit at training time (512 for BERT), and compute per pair grows with sequence length. For long documents, chunk and take the max (or another aggregate) instead of hoping truncation keeps the right part.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Encoding, hashing and encryption are three different things
md: A hash of a short or guessable value is not secret. There are only 10,000 four-digit PINs; hashing all of them takes a fraction of a second, so a stored SHA-256 of a PIN is as good as the PIN. Lesson 11 covers how passwords must be stored instead.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: RSA with tiny numbers: encryption, signing and padding
md: If you ever write pow(m, e, n) in production code you have built textbook RSA. Call a library's OAEP or PSS function, or better, avoid RSA encryption entirely and use an elliptic-curve key exchange plus an AEAD.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Hopper mainloops: TMA, stages and warp specialization
md: A Hopper CUTLASS mainloop is a ring of shared memory stages: a producer warp keeps TMA loads ahead, consumer warpgroups run wgmma on full stages, and full and empty barriers pass ownership of each stage back and forth.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Worked example: what a CXL access costs
md: Treat CXL memory as a far NUMA node: same instructions, same caching, about 70 to 100 ns more per miss for a nearby device, bandwidth comparable to a DDR channel per x8 link. Whether it is a win depends on how many misses you send there.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Counting cache lines: the traffic model and the padding bonus
md: Traffic ratio for a streaming loop is $S/k$: record size over bytes touched. For random access to whole records, the ratio flips against SoA by up to the number of fields.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Why distributed bugs refuse to reproduce
md: DST makes a run a pure function of (code, seed). Faults can then be as aggressive and random as you like, because any failure they provoke can be replayed exactly by re-running one seed.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Sampling: predict every mask, keep the confident, remask the rest
md: A sampling step is: one forward pass over the whole sequence, a guess at every masked slot, then keep the k most confident guesses and remask the rest. The schedule fixes k per step; the confidence ranking decides the order.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Moving the KV cache: bytes, links and overlap
md: Transfer cost = prompt tokens x bytes per token / bandwidth. Grouped-query attention, layer-wise streaming and placement on fast links make it small; slow links and long prompts at high rates make it the bottleneck.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Why DPO skips the reward model and the RL loop
md: DPO is not "RLHF without a reward". It fits the same Bradley-Terry reward model, just parameterized through the policy. It also inherits the KL objective's $\beta$. What it removes is the separate reward network and on-policy sampling during training.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Why a live data migration needs four careful phases
md: Turning on dual writes does not make the stores identical. It only covers objects written *after* the switch. Objects that are never updated again stay only in the old store until the backfill copies them.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Why run your tracing logic inside the kernel
md: eBPF lets you run your own logic at the moment an event happens, inside the kernel, with a load-time proof that it cannot crash or hang the machine. bpftrace makes that a one-liner: probe, optional filter, action, and maps that summarize in the kernel.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Fewer operations and fewer weights, then shipping it
md: Pruning does not automatically make a model smaller or faster. The LiteRT docs state that pruned models are the same size on disk and have the same latency; they only compress better. You get size savings from a sparse format or compression, and speed only from kernels or hardware that skip zeros. With 8-bit values plus 8-bit gaps, sparse storage only wins once more than half the weights are zero.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Budget forcing, effort levels and hard caps at inference
md: A small output-token cap is not a cheap way to get short reasoning. The model does not know about the cap, so it can be cut off mid-thought, and you pay for the thinking tokens with nothing to show. Use the effort or budget control that the model was trained to respond to.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Neural NILM, seq2point, and the unseen-house problem
md: Every NILM method injects prior knowledge to resolve an unidentifiable sum. Hart hand-designs it (step signatures), FHMMs encode it as state machines, and neural nets learn it from sub-metered houses. The test that matters is a house the model never saw.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Job titles: taxonomies, seniority and embeddings
md: General-purpose embedding models do not know your abbreviations (`SWE` software engineer, `SDET` software development engineer in test, `RN` registered nurse) and blur words that share context (`sales engineer` vs `software engineer`). Expand abbreviations before embedding, match against many alternate titles rather than one label, and keep an *unknown* outcome instead of forcing the nearest code.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: The winner's curse: why the best public score is too high
md: Misconception: "we never trained on the test queries, so the number is clean." Choosing among variants by their test score is training with a very small model: one decision per comparison. A hundred prompt tweaks checked against the same 50 queries is a hundred-way fit.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: From bug to control: why exploit mitigations exist
md: A mitigation does not remove the bug. It removes one *route* from the bug to control. Patch the bug, prefer memory-safe languages for new code, and treat mitigations as the layer that protects you from the bugs you have not found yet.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: What each mitigation does not stop, and where to practise
md: Combine layers so their blind spots do not line up: canary plus shadow stack or PAC for returns, CFI for forward edges, full RELRO for the GOT, PIE with high-entropy ASLR and no leaks, tagging or hardened allocators for the heap, and a sandbox around anything that parses untrusted input. Then keep fixing bugs.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: FedAvg exactly, worked on three clients over two rounds
md: A common misreading is that FedAvg averages the clients' answers. It averages their **parameters**. In this problem the sample-weighted average of the three local optima is 1.667 and the plain average is 2.0, while the true optimum is 2.3. Averaging models that have fully solved their own problems gives the wrong model.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: ACORN-1: expand at search time instead of build time
md: ACORN-$\gamma$ and ACORN-1 run the same search strategy, predicate subgraph traversal. They differ only in *where* the denser neighborhood comes from: stored at build time (ACORN-$\gamma$, faster search, slower build) or reconstructed from two-hop lookups at query time (ACORN-1, cheap build, somewhat slower search).

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: Counting the work: FLOPs, bytes, and the exponential unit
md: Misconception: "attention is two GEMMs, so it runs at GEMM speed." The softmax between them is cheap in FLOPs but runs on units hundreds of times slower than the tensor cores. FP8 makes it worse: matmul throughput doubles while exponential throughput stays the same.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Crossing lines and why the learned paths curve
md: Straight training targets do not mean straight sampling paths. Each conditional path is a line, but the marginal flow, which is what the network learns and what sampling follows, curves wherever many lines cross.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: What 8 and 4 bits can hold: E4M3, E5M2 and E2M1
md: "FP8 training" does not mean every tensor is FP8. In the FP8 paper, DeepSeek-V3 and the NVFP4 report alike, only the *inputs* to GEMMs are FP8. GEMM outputs come out in BF16 or FP32, and normalizations, softmax, the master weights and optimizer state stay in higher precision.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: The write-ahead rule: flush the log first, pages later
md: The write-ahead rule, in PostgreSQL's words: changes to data files must be written only after the log records describing them have been flushed to permanent storage. A commit is durable once its commit record is flushed; data pages can be written much later.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Seeds, dictionaries and corpus minimisation
md: Seeds change results more than people expect. Klees et al. (lesson 9) found AFLFast produced over 1,000 crashing inputs on `nm` from an empty seed but only 24 from a small valid seed, statistically the same as AFL's 23. Always report which seeds you used.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Symbolic and concolic execution: solving for the input
md: Symbolic execution turns 'find an input that reaches here' into a math problem: collect the path condition, give it to an SMT solver, get a concrete input. Concolic execution keeps one foot in real execution to stay practical.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Jaro-Winkler, trigrams and token scorers on the same pairs
md: `partial_ratio` produces false positives on short strings: `fuzz.partial_ratio("ai", "said hello")` is 100 because `ai` appears inside `said`. Likewise `token_set_ratio` returns 100 for any subset, so `google` vs `google cloud platform team` is a perfect score. Use these scorers with a minimum length or combine them with other evidence.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Verification: accepting a match only when the odds reach a billion
md: The verification math assumes stray detections are independent and uniform. Satellite trails, diffraction spikes (the straight rays that bright stars show because light bends around the supports holding the telescope's secondary mirror), plate scratches and dense clusters violate that, so false positives there are far more common than the formula predicts. Mask streaks before solving.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Better cells on the sphere: S2 cubes and H3 hexagons
md: All three systems are the same idea as lesson 3: name cells with integers, cover the query with cells, read those cells, then refine. S2 and H3 trade geohash's simplicity for cells that behave well everywhere on the sphere, including poles and the antimeridian.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Best fit, splitting and merging inside segments
md: Misconception: "OOM with lots of reserved memory means a leak." Often it is fragmentation: the free memory exists but in holes smaller than the request, inside segments that cannot be released because a live tensor still occupies part of them.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: How a warp's 32 addresses become 32-byte sectors
md: **Misconception:** coalescing requires thread k to read element k. It does not. The Programming Guide notes that permuted access within the same 32-byte segments is just as good. What matters is the ratio of bytes used to bytes transferred.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Timeline first: where the 14.52 ms actually goes
md: Remember the order. The timeline sets the denominator for everything else: a kernel that is 4 percent of the wall time can never give you more than 4 percent, however bad its counters look.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: Warps and SIMT: 32 threads, one instruction, and divergence
md: SIMT is not the same as SIMD. In CPU SIMD one instruction works on several values packed into one wide vector register (8 floats in a 256-bit AVX register, for example), and the software sees the vector width and manages lanes itself. In SIMT you write scalar per-thread code and the hardware groups it. Correctness never depends on warps; performance does, much like cache lines.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Community summaries and map-reduce global search
md: Global search is not cheap per query. The docs call it resource-intensive: the map step makes one LLM call per batch of reports, so lower (more detailed) levels cost more calls. Picking the community level is a quality versus cost dial.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Why PPO is costly for LLMs and what GRPO removes
md: GRPO removes the **critic**, not the reward. In DeepSeekMath, GRPO was trained against a learned reward model. Rule-based verifiable rewards came to the fore with DeepSeek-R1. GRPO and RLVR are separate ideas that work well together.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: Joining realtime to the schedule and propagating delay
md: Prediction at a stop = scheduled instant + the delay from the nearest StopTimeUpdate at or before it, unless that update is NO_DATA. SKIPPED stops are passed through, earlier stops are never filled in, and an absolute time beats a delay.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: What a side channel is: secrets leaking through how code runs
md: Misconception: "adding a random delay hides the timing". Noise only forces the attacker to average more measurements; Paul Kocher showed in 1996 that the number of measurements grows with the square of the noise (lesson 2). Remove the dependency instead.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: What 4 KiB pages cost a 16 GiB working set
md: These are load counts, not latencies. CPUs keep paging-structure caches and multiple TLB levels with model-specific sizes, so a real miss usually skips some loads. The ratios show the direction of the effect; only a measurement on your hardware gives the size.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Why a fixed-size state forgets and a KV cache does not
md: The hybrid bet: SSM or linear-attention layers do most of the sequence mixing cheaply, and a handful of full attention layers act as an exact lookup into the past. The Mamba-2 authors put it as SSM layers being a general sequence-to-sequence map while attention layers are "a retrieval mechanism to quickly refer to previous tokens".

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: A cross-encoder reranks the fused shortlist
md: Fusion is about **recall of the shortlist** (the share of relevant documents that make it in); reranking is about **precision at the top** (the share of the top few that are relevant). Fused-list quality caps what the reranker can achieve, and rerank depth N trades latency for the chance to rescue documents fused low.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Zones and conduits: the ISA/IEC 62443 way to segment
md: A conduit is a promise in two parts: only these services, between only these zones. Write it down as a table, enforce it with firewalls or gateways, and monitor it so that anything outside the table becomes an alert.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: IT/OT convergence: Colonial, Oldsmar, Unitronics, Volt Typhoon
md: CISA's 2025 primary mitigations for OT read like a summary of these four cases: remove OT connections to the public internet, change default passwords, secure remote access, segment IT and OT, and practise operating manually.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Rejecting bad matches, warping, and direct ECC alignment
md: Those border zeros look like a dark region in the warped image, and subtracting it from the reference flags a band of fake change along the edges. Warp an all-ones image with the same H to get a validity mask, and ignore pixels outside it.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Preparation: plan, people, contacts, retainers and logs
md: A plan that has never been exercised is a guess. The HSE review recommends testing plans against a catastrophic ransomware scenario in which all IT, all security tools and all usual communication channels are unavailable for weeks.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Building a timeline: super timelines, plaso and a worked merge
md: Never mix time zones silently. Convert everything to UTC at ingestion and keep the original value and its assumed zone, so that a later correction (a server set to the wrong zone, a drifting clock) can be applied and explained.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Heartland and TalkTalk: SQL injection as the way in
md: Both breaches started with a well-known bug class in a web page, and both turned into something much larger: lateral movement into a payment network in one case, and a forgotten set of acquired pages exposing a customer database in the other. You cannot fix pages you do not know you run, so asset inventory is a defence against injection too.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Submitting, waiting and how the kernel runs a request
md: A classic bug: `char buf[4096];` on the stack of a function that preps a read, submits, and returns. The kernel later writes 4096 bytes into a stack frame that now belongs to someone else. Buffers belong to the kernel from submission until the matching CQE.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: Cross-thread frees, idle caches and returning memory
md: Published benchmarks (including those in mimalloc's README and report) measure specific workloads. Allocator rankings change with object sizes, thread counts and cross-thread patterns. Measure throughput, p99 latency (the 99th percentile: the time that 99 percent of requests beat) and RSS (resident set size, the memory actually held in RAM) on your own service, with production-like load, before and after switching.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Why the winner changes when the shape changes
md: A common bug is a tuning cache keyed on the kernel name alone, or on batch size only. It never misses, so it never re-tunes, and it silently serves a configuration chosen for a different shape. The symptom is a kernel that is fast in the benchmark that tuned it and mediocre everywhere else.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Worked example: how SPDK reaches 10 million IOPS on one thread
md: Measure with the right tool. SPDK reports up to 2.6 times more IOPS per core using its own `perf` example tool than using fio (the Flexible I/O Tester, the standard Linux storage benchmark) with the SPDK plugin for 4 KiB random reads, because fio's flexibility costs cycles. A slow benchmark harness can hide a fast driver.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Why a teacher's soft targets beat one-hot labels
md: The teacher's knowledge is its input-to-output mapping, including how much probability it gives to each wrong answer. Distillation transfers that mapping by using the teacher's full output distribution as the training target.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Sizing the KV cache of Llama 3 8B, and why it caps batch size
md: A common slip is to use `num_attention_heads` (32) instead of `num_key_value_heads` (8) for a GQA model like Llama 3. That overstates its cache by 4x.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Keeping fewer tokens: windows, attention sinks and heavy hitters
md: Accumulated sums favor older tokens, which have had more steps to collect attention. In the toy, every later token entered with a tiny sum and was evicted within a few steps of leaving the recent slots.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Finding a prefix across tiers, requests and engines
md: Offload tiers are a bigger prefix cache with the same keys. A hit is the longest contiguous prefix found across all tiers; everything after the first gap is prefill.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: HLC in production: 64 bits, bounded c, and uncertainty
md: HLC gives causality-respecting timestamps that look like wall time and fit in 64 bits. It does not make clocks agree: systems that need real-time guarantees still have to assume a skew bound and either wait it out (Spanner) or retry within it (CockroachDB).

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Why reasoning in word tokens is a bottleneck
md: Misconception: Coconut does not shrink the model or skip layers. Each latent step is still a full forward pass through all layers. What it removes is the trip through the LM head, sampling and the embedding table between passes.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Pause tokens, filler dots, recurrent depth and Coconut's costs
md: Choose by what the extra slots carry. Fixed pause or filler embeddings add width within one pass. Coconut's fed-back hidden states and written CoT add serial depth across passes. Recurrent depth adds serial depth inside the network without any extra tokens.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: Inserts, disks and when a learned index pays off
md: Bigtable's lesson: if you control the layout, make the data follow the model instead of making the model follow the data. Then the prediction is never wrong and there is no last-mile search across blocks.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: LambdaRank: weight each pair by what a swap does to NDCG
md: A lambda is a RankNet pair gradient scaled by how much the metric would change if the pair swapped. Pairs that cannot change the top of the list get almost no weight.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Gated DeltaNet: targeted writes plus fast forgetting
md: Gated DeltaNet's one-line change: decay first with a data-dependent $\alpha_t$, then do a delta-rule write with $\beta_t$. $\alpha_t\to0$ clears memory at a context switch; $\alpha_t\to1$ keeps it and lets the delta rule edit single associations.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Services, systemd and cron: what runs without anyone logged in
md: A cron job run by root that executes a script writable by another user is a privilege escalation waiting to happen: whoever can edit the script chooses what root runs every night. When auditing, check the permissions of every file a root job calls, not only the crontab line.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: A basic hardening checklist and where to practise
md: Patch, expose less, use keys, grant little, keep logs off the box and keep baselines. Each step is simple; together they turn most of the attacks in this course from silent root into a noisy, short-lived event.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: LLM judges for generation: modes, biases and fixes
md: A safe default for generation judging: pairwise or rubric grading with the explanation before the verdict; both orders, with disagreement treated as a tie; report and control length; a judge outside the model families being compared; and a human-labelled subset to measure agreement before every major change.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Continuous batching: scheduling every iteration
md: Continuous batching does **not** mean padding requests to a common length. The tokens are packed with no padding, and only attention looks at per-request boundaries. TensorRT-LLM's in-flight batching explicitly requires packed (unpadded) inputs for this reason.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: How vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM put it together
md: Strip away names and every engine is the same loop: a scheduler spending a per-step token budget, a block allocator answering whether it fits, and a policy for when it does not. The engines differ mainly in that last policy and in how they reuse cached blocks.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Designing the filter schema: enums, ranges and nulls
md: A required, non-nullable field such as `salary_max: integer` forces the model to produce a number even when the user said nothing about salary. Constrained decoding guarantees *some* integer, so you get an invented bound (for example 0, or a number copied from a few-shot example) and a filter that silently removes good results.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Latency: the dependency chain decides, not the call count
md: Parallelism is a latency lever, not a cost lever. Running 100 pointwise calls at once reads the same 22,000 tokens as running them one by one, and on a hosted API it uses up rate limits faster.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Pairwise ranking prompting: allpairs, sorting and sliding
md: Pairwise preferences are not guaranteed to be transitive: the model can prefer A over B, B over C and C over A. Allpair just counts wins and copes; sorting algorithms assume a consistent comparator, so their output can depend on which pairs they happened to ask. The PRP paper reports robust results anyway but flags this as an open issue.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: ORB: binary descriptors compared with XOR and popcount
md: Float descriptors (SIFT) are compared with L2 distance; binary descriptors (ORB) with Hamming distance. Binary descriptors trade some distinctiveness for much cheaper extraction, storage and comparison.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The ABA problem: when a matching CAS is still wrong
md: Garbage collection does not make ABA go away in general. Michael points out that if a program moves the same node back and forth between two lock-free stacks, a stale CAS can still succeed even with perfect GC. What GC (and the schemes in lesson 6) do prevent is the special case where ABA comes from *freeing and reusing* a node someone still references.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: How accurate is this really, and by which metric
md: Vocabulary trap. "Parsing accuracy" in the 2019 benchmark means grouping, not token-level correctness. Modern papers reserve **PA**, short for parsing accuracy, for the stricter message-level metric where every static token *and* every parameter must be identified correctly, and use **GA** for grouping. A number quoted without its metric is worthless, so always ask: grouping or tokens, per message or per template?

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: The pipeline: collect, ship, parse, enrich, store
md: Monitor the pipeline like a production service: events per source per hour, parse-failure rate, queue depth, and the age of the newest event. A sensor that stops sending looks exactly like a quiet, safe network.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Threat hunting and the Pyramid of Pain: the FireEye alert
md: Use indicators (hashes, IPs, domains) for fast, cheap blocking and for searching history after a report is published. Invest your engineering time in behaviour detections, because they are the ones that still work next month.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Attention memory and Ring Attention
md: Online softmax makes attention over KV blocks order-independent. Ring Attention exploits that: queries stay put, KV blocks travel around the ring, and each host needs memory proportional to its block, not to the full sequence.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Training for any loop count: random depth and truncated backprop
md: Random iteration counts teach one set of weights to work at many depths. Truncated backprop through only the last $k$ iterations keeps training memory independent of $r$, while the input injection still sends gradient to the prelude.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: QLoRA: fine-tuning on top of a 4-bit base model
md: QLoRA separates a storage type (NF4, 4 bits) from a compute type (BF16). Only the adapters are trained, so quantization error in the frozen base can be compensated by the adapters, and memory drops by about 4x versus a 16-bit base.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Hidden, not gone: relearning, probing and quantization attacks
md: A model that passes forget-set benchmarks in full precision can fail them after an ordinary 4-bit conversion that a user applies for deployment. Any release that relies on unlearning should evaluate the quantized versions people will actually run.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Reading x86-64 assembly: registers and core instructions
md: You do not need to read every instruction. Analysts skim for calls (what API is used?), compares and conditional jumps (what decision is made?), and constants (what string, size or key is used?).

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Indicators of compromise and the Pyramid of Pain
md: Hashes and IPs are for fast, cheap blocking and for searching history. Artifacts, tools and TTPs are what keep working next month. Report both, but build your detections near the top of the pyramid.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Why one GPU cannot train a 175B model, and the five ways to split it
md: Every axis splits something different: TP splits matrices, PP splits layers, DP splits the batch, CP splits the sequence, EP splits experts. Choosing a configuration means choosing which communication you can afford on which link.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Free memory you cannot use: two kinds of fragmentation
md: Internal fragmentation is waste inside handed-out blocks (a rounding cost). External fragmentation is free memory split into holes too small to use (a placement and lifetime cost). Both are measured against live data, and the number depends on when you measure.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Acquire and release: publishing data across threads
md: There is no "acquire store" or "release load". Release only affects stores and Acquire only affects loads; SeqCst cannot create them either. A Release store and a Release store never synchronize with each other.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Epoch-based reclamation: free garbage two epochs later
md: EBR pays per operation, not per node, and needs no per-node announcement. In exchange, a single thread stalled while pinned blocks all reclamation, so garbage is unbounded.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: The call stack: frames, return addresses and saved frame pointers
md: The stack grows toward lower addresses, so people often assume an overflowing array also spills downward. It does not. `strcpy`, `gets` and loops write from `buf[0]` toward `buf[7]` and beyond, which means toward *higher* addresses: straight into the saved frame pointer and the return address of the same frame.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Why re-ID needs an embedding space, not a classifier
md: A subtle limit of contrastive loss: it pulls every same-identity pair toward distance 0, so it tries to squash all images of one person onto a single point. The authors of FaceNet (Google's 2015 face recognition system, next lesson) argued that a triplet loss is better suited, because it only asks same-identity images to be closer than other identities, letting one person's images spread out along a region.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: When the optimizer deletes the code you meant to time
md: Misconception: "returning or summing the result is enough". Using the output defeats dead-code elimination, but not constant folding. The input must also come from somewhere the compiler cannot see through. JMH's constant-folding sample says to read inputs from non-final fields of a state object, and warns against making them `final` even when your IDE suggests it.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Miles in one picture: slime's loop built for frontier scale
md: The Miles docs do not publish a line-by-line diff against slime. This course teaches what Miles documents and measures; do not conclude from it that slime lacks any particular feature.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Why hand-tuned policies leave a gap: LRU versus Belady's MIN
md: MIN is not a policy you can deploy, and it is not what learned caches try to predict exactly. It is a **yardstick**. Its value is telling you how big the gap is. On six production CDN traces with a 1 TB cache, the LRB authors measured a 25 to 40% gap in byte miss ratio (the fraction of requested bytes the cache could not serve) between MIN and the best online policies they tested.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Low-rank joint compression: cache one latent, rebuild every head
md: MLA is not a compression applied to an already trained model's cache, like PCA (principal component analysis, which finds the few directions that capture most of the variation in a set of vectors) run on stored keys. The down- and up-projections are ordinary weights learned from scratch during pretraining. Converting an existing MHA or GQA model to MLA needs extra fine-tuning work (see lesson 5).

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Thousands of adapters: S-LoRA's unified paging and loading
md: Unified Paging is not magic capacity. Adapter pages and KV pages come from the same pool, so many large adapters active at once shrink the space for KV cache and therefore the batch size. That is why clustering and rank choices still matter.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: Why one scorer cannot be both cheap and accurate
md: Each stage has a different job. The first stage must not lose relevant documents (recall); precision barely matters there, because later stages discard junk. The last stage must put the best documents on top (precision at the top) and only has to be good on a short list.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Why lookahead helps, and where it does not
md: MTP reweights training toward decisions that matter for the continuation. It helps most on generative tasks such as code, at larger model sizes, with n tuned to the data; it is not a free win on every benchmark.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: SOAP: run Adam in the coordinates Shampoo discovers
md: SOAP is not cheap in memory. Per $m \times n$ layer it stores $L$, $Q_L$, $R$, $Q_R$, $M$, $V$ plus the gradient: $2m^2 + 2n^2 + 3mn$ numbers, the same as Distributed Shampoo, against $3mn$ for AdamW. For a $4096 \times 4096$ layer that is 117.4M versus 50.3M floats. Variants with a one-sided rotation and Adafactor's factored $V$ cut this to $2\min(m,n)^2 + 2mn$.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: muTransfer in practice: what transfers and what it saved
md: Don't expect dropout or weight decay tuned on a small proxy to be optimal for a much larger model trained on different amounts of data. The paper also notes that muTransfer may not be enough for fine-tuning on small datasets, where regularization matters most.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: Locks in real systems: kernels, priorities and choices
md: User-space spin locks lack the kernel's guarantee. A user thread cannot disable preemption, so a pure spin lock in an application can always spin against a preempted holder. Prefer the platform mutex, which already spins briefly before sleeping.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Write skew: the bug that snapshot isolation lets through
md: Snapshot isolation prevents conflicts between writes to the same row. Write skew slips through because the conflicting pair is a read and a write to *different* rows.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: Transformer taggers and subword alignment
md:
Two alignment bugs cost real F1 and neither one crashes.

Labelling continuation pieces with `I-X` instead of -100 teaches the model that spans can start and continue inside a word, which leaks into the decoder.

Evaluating on pieces instead of words changes the number of gold entities, so your F1 is not comparable to anyone else's. Map back to words first, then score.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: pHash: hashing the low frequencies of a DCT
md: aHash compares pixels with the mean, dHash compares neighbors, pHash compares low-frequency DCT coefficients with their median. All three are **global**: they describe the whole frame at fixed positions, which is why resizing and tone changes are cheap to survive and crops, flips and rotations are not.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Where the attacker stands: on-path, off-path and on your LAN
md: Know the position before you pick the defence. Encryption (TLS) defeats on-path reading and rewriting of content. Unpredictable numbers (random ports, sequence numbers, IDs) defeat off-path guessing. Switch features such as MAC limiting, DHCP snooping and ARP inspection stop local attackers from becoming on-path.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: RST injection and the history of TCP session hijacking
md: Address-based trust is the real bug behind classic hijacking. Any system that grants access because a packet claims a source IP (old rsh, IP allow lists alone, zone transfers allowed by address) is relying on something an attacker can forge. Use cryptographic authentication.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: IP addresses, subnets and CIDR
md: Prefix length decides everything: which addresses are "local" (same subnet, reached directly) and which need a router. If you can turn /27 into a network address, a broadcast address and a host count, you can read any firewall rule or scan scope.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Why some memory is farther away than other memory
md: Remote memory is not slow like disk. It is the same DRAM, reached through one more hop, typically tens of percent slower per miss. The bigger danger is usually *bandwidth*: when all hot data sits on one node, one memory controller serves every socket while the others idle.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Keeping threads near their data: pinning, balancing and diagnosis
md: Balancing is not free. The kernel docs say the unmapping and extra faults cost overhead that is *ideally* offset by better locality, with no universal guarantee, and that it should be disabled when the workload is already bound to NUMA nodes. Workloads that are already pinned and carefully placed are the natural candidates to turn it off.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Removing duplicates: greedy NMS and DETR's set prediction
md: Duplicates are handled either after the fact by NMS, a hand-tuned greedy filter on IoU, or during training by one-to-one Hungarian matching, which teaches the model itself to emit one box per object.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Committing to object storage: metadata, CAS and fencing
md: Leases and timeouts alone do not fence. A paused process cannot notice that its lease expired while it was paused, so its next write happens anyway. Safety comes from the **storage rejecting** the stale writer: a conditional PUT on a slot the new writer already claimed.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Cardinality: labels multiply, and a histogram multiplies again
md: Never put an unbounded set in a label. The naming guide names the usual offenders: do not use labels to store dimensions with high cardinality, such as user IDs, email addresses, or other unbounded sets of values. Raw URLs with query strings, trace ids, error message strings and timestamps belong on the same list.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Reading a line: CRNN features and CTC decoding
md: Merging repeats happens **before** removing blanks. Doing it in the other order would turn b - o - o k into b o o k and then merge the o's into 'bok'.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: SELinux: labels, types and the policy that decides
md: Two habits defeat SELinux: switching it to permissive "to make the app work", and feeding every denial to `audit2allow`, a tool that writes allow rules from log lines. The SELinux Notebook warns that new rules "may start opening holes". First ask whether the label is wrong (restorecon) or a boolean exists for the need.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Putting it together: one service, many layers
md: Assume each layer will fail and ask what the next one still guarantees: least privilege inside the program (privsep, drops), MAC around it, seccomp and capabilities on its kernel access, namespaces and cgroups around its view, and a separate kernel when the code is hostile. Patching is the layer under all of them.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: What CI does when you open a pull request
md: CI is a contract written in the repo: on these events, on these machines, run these commands, and block the merge unless they exit with status 0. Read `.github/workflows/` before your first PR to a project.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: What a reviewer is deciding: the code-health standard
md: Misconception: a reviewer who leaves 15 comments is blocking you on all 15. Often most are optional. If the reviewer did not say which ones block the merge, ask instead of guessing.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Where a project's rules live and how GitHub finds them
md: Read in this order before you touch code: LICENSE (can you contribute at all), CONTRIBUTING (how), CODE_OF_CONDUCT (how to behave), SECURITY (if your finding is a vulnerability). Ten minutes of reading avoids a rejected PR.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Keeping a branch current: rebase onto upstream/main
md: Rebase rewrites history. The rule from Pro Git, the free Git book on git-scm.com: do not rebase commits that exist outside your repository and that people may have based work on. Your own PR branch is the usual exception, which is why the next lesson's force-push needs care, not a ban.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: No license means no permission: what a license grants
md: Public is not the same as open source. Code you can read on GitHub with no license file is all rights reserved, and so is a snippet whose license you never checked.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: The DCO: certifying every commit with Signed-off-by
md: CLA: one signed agreement per person or company, granting rights up front. DCO: no agreement, just a per-commit certification of origin via Signed-off-by, checked mechanically by email match.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Map the repository before you read a line of it
md: A common mistake is to fix a bug inside a generated file. Your edit is overwritten the next time the generator runs, and reviewers will reject it. When a file says *do not edit*, find its input (here `src/commands/get.json`) in the build rule and change that instead.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Shrinking a failing program by hand
md: Every cut is an experiment: remove, rerun, compare to the original failure. Keep cuts that preserve the exact error; undo the rest.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: One logical change per PR, and every commit builds
md: If the project squash-merges PRs, your intermediate commits disappear from the main branch anyway, and the PR as a whole becomes one commit. That makes **one logical change per PR** even more important: the squash cannot separate a fix from a speedup after the fact.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Block tables: virtual memory for the KV cache
md: Paging is not free. The paper measured 20 to 26% higher attention kernel latency than FasterTransformer's kernel, from block-table lookups, extra branches and variable lengths. It still wins end to end because only the attention operator pays, and the larger batch more than makes up for it.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: When authorisation is unclear: the Iowa courthouse arrests
md: Ambiguity is what got two professionals arrested. Write down: who owns each target, who signed for it, when testing may happen, who outside the client has been told, and two 24/7 ways to reach someone who can confirm it.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Why profilers sample stacks instead of timing every call
md: A sampling profiler answers one question: what fraction of CPU samples had this function on the stack? It is cheap because work happens per sample, not per call, and it is approximate because it is a sample.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Why a finished store is not yet durable
md: Common misconception: "unflushed stores are lost on a crash." Some are, some are not, and the hardware chooses. Treat each dirty cache line as independently maybe-persisted. Flushes give you a lower bound on what is durable, never an upper bound.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Envelope, header and display name: why spoofing works
md: Authentication checks answer "was this domain's use authorised?", never "is this message honest?". A display-name spoof or lookalike domain passes them cleanly. Defences need both: DMARC against exact-domain spoofing, and human-facing cues plus process rules for the rest.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: How the compiler lays out a struct, field by field
md: Two rules give every struct layout: **each field's offset is a multiple of its alignment**, and **the struct's size is a multiple of its own alignment** (the largest field alignment). Everything else, including all the padding, follows from these.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Real-time tracking, 3D lifting and joint angles for apps
md: Keypoints are noisy, especially when occluded. Before writing rules on them: check per-keypoint visibility or score, prefer 3D world landmarks or a side view for sagittal angles (bends in the side-view plane that splits the body into left and right) such as the knee, smooth over a few frames, and use two thresholds (hysteresis) rather than one.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Latency versus bandwidth: two different walls
md: Common misconception: "faster RAM will speed up my tree or hash-chain lookups." Faster transfer rates raise peak bandwidth, but a dependent chain of misses uses a tiny fraction of it. Its cost is set by latency, which has improved far more slowly.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Credentials are the real currency: where they live on a host
md: Misconception: "we have MFA, so stolen hashes and tickets don't matter." Multi-factor authentication protects the sign-in that asks for it, usually remote access and cloud portals. Inside a Windows network, NTLM and Kerberos authentication to a file server or another workstation uses the hash or ticket directly and does not prompt for a second factor.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Failure modes, evaluation, and why some labs skip PRMs
md: PRMs give denser, more precise feedback than outcome checks, but they are learned models: they can be exploited by search and RL, they degrade under distribution shift, and their labels (human, MC, or judge) each carry their own noise. Use them where search or reranking pays off and keep the final-answer verifier in the loop.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Training per-slice codebooks and encoding a vector
md: Common misconception: a PQ code is a lossless compression of the vector. It is not. Two different vectors with the same code are indistinguishable to the index, and every distance computed from codes inherits the quantization error.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Twenty letters, one backbone: the design problem
md:
Two separate objects, and you must keep them apart:

- **sequence**: which of the 20 amino acids sits at each position (discrete, one symbol per residue)
- **backbone**: where the N, CA, C and O atoms of every residue sit in 3D space (continuous coordinates)

The chain folds into one preferred backbone shape, and that shape is what gives the protein its function.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Files, functions and exceptions: scripts that survive bad input
md: Never write a bare `except:` or `except Exception: pass` around a whole script. It also swallows bugs in your own code and even Ctrl+C in the bare form, so the script reports "no alerts" when it actually crashed on line 2. Catch the specific exception you expect, at the place you can handle it, and let everything else fail loudly.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Encodings: base64, hex and URL encoding, and why attackers use them
md: Encoding is reversible formatting, not secrecy. Normalize data (decode, lowercase, refang) before matching it, and expect attackers to stack encodings to slip past exact-match rules.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Expanding with models: doc2query, query2doc and HyDE
md: These numbers come from specific benchmarks (MS MARCO, TREC DL) and specific models. Measure on your own queries with judged results before adopting any expansion: a gain on average can still hurt many individual queries.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: RaBitQ indexing: normalize, rotate randomly, keep the signs
md: RaBitQ indexing: center and normalize, apply one random rotation, store the sign bits plus two floats per vector. The codebook is the rotated hypercube, so no k-means training is needed.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Consensus in production: reads, membership, timeouts
md: Consensus is safe without any timing assumptions; timing only buys availability. Every production feature here (reads, reconfiguration, Pre-Vote) is checked against the same question: can two majorities that do not overlap make conflicting decisions?

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Document, query and interaction signals: freshness, popularity, clicks
md: Shape raw signals before the model sees them: turn age into a decaying freshness, counts into logs or rates, and remember that query-only features can only matter through interactions.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Is the difference real? Paired tests, effect sizes, many systems
md: Compare systems on per-query differences, with a paired t-test or randomization test, and report the mean difference with a confidence interval and effect size. With many systems, control the familywise error instead of running dozens of independent tests.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: WebSocket: one HTTP upgrade, then a two-way framed stream
md: Masking is **not encryption**: the key travels in the same frame. RFC 6455 requires it (even over TLS) so that a script in the browser cannot choose the exact bytes on the wire. Without it, an attacker could craft upgraded traffic that a broken proxy reads as an HTTP request and caches, then serves that forged response to other users: the cache-poisoning attack in section 10.3. Use `wss://` (TLS) for confidentiality.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: From a sparse rating matrix to item-to-item recommendations
md: Item-to-item CF scales because the heavy work (the similar-items table) is offline, and the online step only touches the handful of items in one user's history.

courseTitle: Measuring size from a reference marker
lessonTitle: Why a photo has no scale until you add a reference
md: A reference object gives you scale only for points at its depth (more precisely, on its plane). Everything else in the image has a different pixels-per-mm.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: How the planner chooses: join order search and row estimates
md: The same study found that most of PostgreSQL's timeouts came from a nested-loop join without an index, chosen because a tiny row estimate made it look cheapest. When the real input was large, its rows x rows work exploded. A cost-only choice ignores how risky a plan is if the estimate is wrong.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: When a high score stops meaning a solved task
md: The reward is an imperfect measurement of the goal. Optimization pressure flows to wherever the measurement and the goal disagree, so the harder you optimize, the more those disagreements decide what you get.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Assessing risk in practice: from asset list to risk register
md: Multiplying ordinal numbers (ranks, like 1 to 5) treats the gap between 4 and 5 as equal to the gap between 1 and 2, which is rarely true of real losses. Grids are fine for sorting a long list quickly and for talking to non-specialists. They are not fine for deciding whether a USD 300,000 control is worth buying. For that, estimate in money.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: NIST CSF 2.0: six functions, profiles and tiers
md: Misconception: "we implemented the CSF". The CSF lists outcomes, not controls; you cannot install it. Saying you *use* it means you have profiles, owners for the gaps and a review cycle. A slide with the six function names is not alignment.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Compliance as code: policy checks in CI and automatic evidence
md: A control that runs as code on every change is both stronger security and better evidence: the CI logs show it ran on every pull request all year, and the evidence store shows the state on any date an auditor picks. Failing the build is the cheapest moment to fix a compliance gap.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Cyber insurance: what it pays, what it asks, what it excludes
md: Cyber insurance transfers part of the financial tail: forensics, restoration, business interruption, liability. It is priced and conditioned on your controls; misstatements can void claims. Model deductible and limit against your loss distribution, read the exclusions (fraud, war and state-backed attacks), and keep the application as true as your SOC 2.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Weight sync: resharding and moving the bytes every step
md: Sync cost = bytes / bandwidth + resharding. The bytes are fixed by model size and precision; good systems avoid gathering the full model anywhere, send each rank only its shard, and keep the transfer off the critical path.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: Walking the dependency graph to the anomalous frontier
md: Correlation is not causation, and the SRE troubleshooting chapter names the two ways this bites. First, correlated events often share a cause: packet loss in a cluster and failed disks in the same cluster correlate because a power event hit both, not because either caused the other. Second, as you monitor more metrics it becomes inevitable that some will correlate well with your symptom purely by coincidence.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Ties, missing documents and the window size
md: Pagination: in Elasticsearch, if `from + size` (results skipped plus the page length) exceeds `rank_window_size` you get 0 results, and pages are only consistent while `rank_window_size` stays fixed. Changing W re-ranks everything, as the animation shows, so never vary it between page requests.
